To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the use of stiff and stiff and non-stiff methods for integrating combustion rate equations can be more efficient than the use of only stiff methods, but that the use of non-stiff and stiff methods is more efficient than the selective use of non-stif and non-stiff and non-stiff.

the integration of combustion kinetic rate equations can be accelerated by selective use of non-stiff and stiff methods, depending on the problem, and that the use of non-stif methods in the low temperature regime is especially beneficial.

(1) the use of a nonstiff method in the early stages of the reaction and a stiff method in the later stages of the reaction is faster than the application of a stiff method for the entire integration; (2) this is true for both the explicit and the implicit stiff methods; and (3) the implicit stiff method is faster than the explicit one for the entire integration.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of efficient algorithms for integrating chemical kinetic rate equations.
developing a new class of algorithms for solving stiff chemical kinetic problems that is based on a combination of the implicit and explicit methods.
the development of efficient algorithms for integrating combustion kinetics rate equations.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the use of nonstif methods for the low temperature and stiff methods for the high temperature regimes in a typical batch combustion reaction is faster than the exclusive use of either method.
the use of stiff methods is more efficient than the use of nonstif methods for the integration of combustion kinetic rate equations.
the best integration method for the combustion kinetic equations is a method that is stiff in the high-temperature regime and nonstiff in the low-temperature regime.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
a combination of nonstiff, stiff and hybrid methods is the most efficient way for solving combustion problems.
the use of stiff and/or nonstiff integration methods for solving combustion kinetic problems depends upon the particular problem and its characteristics.

a combination of the nonstiff method of Gear (Gear 1971) and the stiff methods of Gear and Petzold (Gear and Petzold 1984) and Vandenberge and Gear (Vandenberge and Petzold, 1984) is superior to either method alone for the problems considered here.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the use of a nonstiff method in combination with a stiff method can lead to a substantial increase in the speed of integration.
the use of nonstif methods is not only possible but desirable for integration of combustion kinetic rate equations.

the use of stiff methods for the initial transient phase and the final steady-state phase of a batch combustion problem is not efficient, while the use of a nonstiff method for the intermediate, transient phase is.
